newsitem.title: USA: Financial scandal rocks troubled Miami again.
newsitem.headline: Financial scandal rocks troubled Miami again.

text.p: Another financial scandal has broken over Miami, a city already so mired in corruption that disgusted residents may abolish it as a municipal entity later this year.
The director of Miami's bustling sea port, who was facing questions about the port's finances, abruptly announced his retirement over the weekend, officials said Monday.

Port Director Carmen Lunetta, 67, made the decision after documents obtained by The Miami Herald showed seaport revenues had been spent on Super Bowl tickets, luxury car rentals and campaign contributions, including contributions to current county commissioners.
Lunetta faxed his retirement letter to Dade County Manager Armando Vidal during the weekend.

On Monday, County Mayor Alex Penelas requested an outside audit of the seaport. He said an internal audit that disclosed a seaport cash flow deficit of $22 million was "troubling and of serious concern to Dade County taxpayers."

Penelas also asked that county comissioners would "seek an assurance of sound financial condition" at the county aviation department, which runs Miami International Airport, and other county departments.
The mayor nevertheless praised Lunetta, noting he "has worked very hard over the past 38 years to make our port a world leader in both the cruise and cargo industries."
Penelas recommended that Lunetta be part of a transition team that will choose his replacement.

Lunetta, port director for 38 years, said he expected to remain a consultant to the county for six months after his resignation takes effect on July 31. He was out of town Monday and would not be back until Tuesday, his secretary said.
The Herald did not directly accuse Lunetta of a crime but said he had jurisdiction over the port's budget and directed a contractor to make some of the questionable expenditures.
The seaport is overseen by Dade County, which believed it to be self-supporting. But last week's audit revealed taxpayer funds had been used to offset port losses for several years.
The port's woes came to light as Miami voters prepared for a Sept. 4 referendum on a proposal to dissolve the city and merge it into the Dade County government.
Gene Stearns, an attorney who supports abolition of Miami as a separate city, said that although the seaport fiasco involves the county, it would boost efforts to have the county take over the city.

"It makes people angry and angry people say 'Throw the rascals out,'" Stearns said. "We're not going to make government less corrupt by dissolving the city. We're just going to reduce the opportunity to steal (by having one less government)."

The city of Miami is only a fragment of the urban sprawl generally known by that name. Most of the greater Miami area is actually run by Dade County authorities or is part of separate cities such as Coral Gables and Miami Beach.
Disgruntled residents forced the referendum after three top city officials resigned to face charges they accepted bribes or solicited kickbacks from city contractors.
After the resignations last fall, an interim city manager discovered that Miami had a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for fiscal 1997.

While Dade County remains solvent, its finances have also been under scrutiny. The Securities and Exchange Commission has subpoenaed documents from both the city and the county and is examining their tax-exempt bond issues.

Dade County Commissioner James Burke, meanwhile, has acknowledged he is a target of Operation Greenpalm, an ongoing federal investigation that resulted in indictments against the three city officials. Burke has denied any wrongdoing.
